clinicalPearls: Caused by Burkholderia mallei, a Gram-negative bacillus, and primarily a disease of solipeds (horses, mules, donkeys) that is transmitted to humans through contact with infected animals or their secretions
Now rare and largely eradicated from many regions, but occupational exposure in veterinarians, farriers and laboratory workers, and its potential as a biothreat agent, keep it clinically relevant
Human infection follows inoculation through broken skin or mucosae or inhalation, with an incubation typically of days to a few weeks
Clinical forms include localised skin and mucosal ulceration with regional lymphadenitis, a suppurative form with abscesses, a pulmonary form, and a rapidly fatal septicaemic form
The organism is closely related to Burkholderia pseudomallei (the cause of melioidosis) and shares its tendency to form deep abscesses and to relapse
Laboratory diagnosis is hazardous, so the laboratory must be warned of the suspected diagnosis to protect staff and use appropriate biosafety containment
Treatment requires prolonged combination antimicrobial therapy modelled on melioidosis regimens because relapse and treatment failure are common
reference.pathophysiology: Burkholderia mallei is a facultative intracellular Gram-negative bacterium that enters through skin, mucosal or respiratory routes. At the entry site it provokes suppurative and later granulomatous inflammation, producing ulcers, nodules and abscesses, and spreads via lymphatics to regional nodes. Haematogenous dissemination can seed the lungs, liver, spleen and other organs with metastatic abscesses, and overwhelming bacteraemia produces a septicaemic syndrome. The ability to survive within phagocytes contributes to chronic, relapsing infection.

Cross-sectional imaging to detect deep abscesses in lungs, liver and spleen
Blood cultures in suspected septicaemic disease
redFlags: Rapidly progressive sepsis with hypotension indicating the septicaemic form
Respiratory distress or extensive pulmonary involvement
Multiple deep abscesses suggesting disseminated disease
Occupational or laboratory exposure raising both diagnostic and public-health concern
Consideration of deliberate release given the organism's biothreat status
reference.prognosis: Untreated septicaemic glanders is frequently fatal, and even with treatment the disease is difficult to eradicate, requiring prolonged combination therapy with a real risk of relapse; localised disease has a better outlook when recognised and treated early.
pitfalls: Failing to warn the laboratory, exposing staff to a hazardous organism
Using short antibiotic courses, which lead to relapse
Confusing glanders with common skin and soft-tissue infection and undertreating
Not eliciting equine or laboratory exposure in the history
Overlooking deep abscesses that require drainage alongside antimicrobials
references: Mandell, Douglas and Bennett's Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases
management: Prolonged antimicrobial therapy modelled on melioidosis, with an intensive intravenous phase using ceftazidime or a carbapenem such as meropenem
Followed by a lengthy oral eradication phase, typically co-trimoxazole with or without doxycycline, to prevent relapse
Surgical drainage of abscesses and debridement of localised suppurative disease as an adjunct to antibiotics
Aggressive supportive and organ-support care with sepsis management for the septicaemic form
Alert the laboratory to the suspected diagnosis and handle specimens under appropriate biosafety containment to protect staff
Notify public health, trace occupational and animal exposures, and consider post-exposure prophylaxis for high-risk contacts
Prolonged follow-up with surveillance for relapse given the organism's intracellular persistence
